stories.title: Louisiana’s accidental blueprint for restoring its coast
stories.summary: In a stretch of southern Louisiana where the coast has been vanishing for a century, the wetlands are actually gaining ground. The Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion, built to fight saltwater intrusion, unexpectedly started rebuilding marsh — a striking reversal tour guide Arthur Matherne can see from his airboat.
stories.extended_summary: Arthur Matherne used to barrel his airboat through channels that held three feet of water. Now they hold three inches — and grasses and oak branches are filling in where open water once stretched. It's a striking reversal in a region that's been losing about 11 square miles of coast a year. The cause sits a few miles away: the Davis Pond Freshwater Diversion, built by the Army Corps of Engineers in 2002 to combat saltwater intrusion. But it did something unexpected — it also started rebuilding the marsh. For a state that's spent decades fighting a losing battle against erosion, this accidental blueprint might be the most hopeful thing on the coast.

That mile is the first new multi-use trail in Jefferson County, with four more coming, and ultimately part of the 3,700-mile Great American Rail-Trail stretching from D.C. to Washington State. Hellbender Preserve opened just a year ago and drew 30,000 visitors in six months. In the Rust Belt, where healthcare isn't always a priority, a free path to get outside and get moving is its own kind of medicine.

stories.summary: A new Anchorage Museum exhibit displays Yup'ik artifacts dating back to the 1500s — excavated by the very village they came from. Lynn Church started the dig at 18. At 36, she's watching her ancestors' masks and tools go on view.
stories.extended_summary: "I was 18 when I started working on this project," Lynn Church says, surveying display cases packed with wooden masks and dolls her own ancestors used generations ago. "I'm 36 now — it's been going on for half of my life." The artifacts, dating to the 1500s, were excavated from a site near the Bering Sea village of Quinhagak and are now on view at the Anchorage Museum in "Nunalleq: The Old Village." Tools, hunting gear, ivory earrings, masks depicting a range of emotions — many still recognizable today. Elizabeth Church pointed to a worn net shuttle: "the same kind of fish net mending tool I used to see my grandfather using."

stories.title: An upscale Somali restaurant at Lake and Nicollet? Owner of Martiya is undaunted and filling tables
stories.summary: Martiya, an upscale Somali restaurant, opened at Lake and Nicollet in south Minneapolis — on the ground floor of an affordable housing complex built after the 2020 riots. Skeptics doubted the location. It sells out daily.
stories.extended_summary: An upscale Somali restaurant at Lake and Nicollet? Plenty of people questioned it — the site sits in an area still working through hard times, on the ground floor of an affordable housing complex built where a Wells Fargo branch was destroyed after George Floyd's killing. Owner Abdirahman Kahin, who ran Afro Deli and Grill for 16 years, opened Martiya anyway. It sells out daily, with limited reservations most evenings. "Martiya came in response to the community's demand," he says — a fine-dining amenity for the East African and Muslim communities, and a statement about who gets to build Minneapolis. Kahin, named the U.S. Small Business Administration's 2023 National Small Business Person of the Year, is betting on his neighborhood.

stories.summary: United Way of Rhode Island just raised the income limit for its heating assistance fund by about $18,000 — meaning a family of four earning up to $115,500 can now qualify. It's a quiet but huge win for working families who make too much for federal aid but still can't cover the basics.
stories.extended_summary: A family of four in Rhode Island earning $115,500 a year can now get help paying for heat — up from $96,450 last season. That's the change United Way of Rhode Island just made to its Good Neighbor Energy Fund, aimed squarely at the working families who fall through the cracks: too much income for federal or state aid, not enough to actually get by. The nonprofit raised the thresholds after its own report found 43% of Rhode Island households can't afford basic expenses. For thousands of families facing the winter, that gap just got a little smaller.

stories.summary: Denver nonprofit We Don't Waste is giving away 80,000 pounds of free potatoes — 40 tons of perfectly fresh spuds rejected by buyers over minor cosmetic flaws. "Potatopalooza" invites anyone in the metro to bring bags, wagons, or a pickup and haul away as many as they can carry.
stories.extended_summary: Clear some space in the pantry: Denver is about to have a lot of potatoes. Two full 53-foot semi-trucks of perfectly fresh spuds were turned away over minor cosmetic flaws — not pretty enough — so the nonprofit We Don't Waste stepped in and took all 80,000 pounds. On Monday, Nov. 2, "Potatopalooza" gives them away free to anyone in the metro area. No limit. Bring bags, boxes, wagons, or a pickup truck and take as many as you can carry. stories.summary: Drake sophomore Felicia Burns, who is blind, found 67 braille inaccuracies across just three campus buildings — including a sign that mislabeled an elevator as the men's restroom — and is now leading a campus-wide audit to fix them.
stories.extended_summary: Felicia Burns was trying to find a class when she ran her finger over an elevator's braille and read 'men's restroom.' That error was one of at least 67 braille inaccuracies she has since documented in only three buildings at Drake University — misspellings, wrong room labels, wrong floor numbers, and 20 missing signs in the Olmsted Center alone. Supported by the Disability Coalition and campus accessibility offices, the sophomore is now leading a full audit of every braille sign on campus, turning a personal frustration into a push to make the bare minimum of ADA compliance actually work.

stories.title: Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them
stories.summary: A Harvard physicist is mapping the 'dark matter' of food — the tens of thousands of natural chemicals we've never tracked. Her team has already cataloged 140,000 molecules, including nearly 7,000 in raw garlic alone.
stories.extended_summary: Raw garlic alone contains almost 7,000 different molecules — and most of them have never been studied for their effects on human health. That's the gap computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is trying to close. Her project, Foodome, uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound ever linked to a food, then flags the ones epidemiology has ignored. So far: about 140,000 molecules cataloged. She calls it 'nutritional dark matter.' The goal isn't to scare people about chemicals — it's to understand how the natural compounds in what we eat interact with our proteins, our microbiome, and our health.

stories.summary: When an elderly woman facing homelessness refused to abandon her 75-pound pit bull, the Community Day Center of Waltham made room for both of them — and months later, she secured permanent housing.
stories.extended_summary: An elderly woman who had lived in the same apartment for two decades was evicted after a rent hike, and every shelter she found turned away her 75-pound pit bull, Callie Jane — a dog she refused to leave, even if it meant sleeping outside. Chloe-Rose Crouch, the 27-year-old executive director of the Community Day Center of Waltham, decided the overnight shelter would accommodate both of them. A few months later, with help from her case manager, the woman secured permanent housing. Today she still brings Callie Jane back to the center for lunch, where guests eagerly greet the dog.

stories.title: Helderberg Lake to get $1M from state to fix its dam, needs a 25% match
stories.summary: After the town board refused to create a tax district, a small lakeside association wrote its own grant application — and on its third try, won $1.06 million from New York State to repair the dam that has been flagged as unsound for nine years.
stories.extended_summary: Nine years ago, New York declared the dam holding back Helderberg Lake 'unsound' — a high-hazard structure whose failure could take out homes, roads, and lives. The lakeside association asked the town to create a tax district to fund repairs; the board said no. So roughly 73 members started their own nonprofit, wrote a grant application themselves, and applied for three straight years. This week, the governor's office announced they'd won $1,064,855 — a public charity operating on less than $50,000 a year just secured a seven-figure state grant to fix the dam. They still need a 25% match, but the finish line is finally in sight.

stories.title: Historic preservationists create virtual 3D model of the Stonewall Inn as it appeared in 1969
stories.summary: Ever wondered what the Stonewall Inn looked like the night it sparked a movement? A new 3D digital model reconstructs the bar's 1969 interior using archival floor plans, oral histories, and photography — the most in-depth resource ever made of the space.
stories.extended_summary: The Stonewall Inn you can walk into today looks almost nothing like the bar that sparked the modern LGBTQ rights movement in 1969. Now you can see the original. Using archival floor plans, oral histories, and photography run through ArcGIS, the NYC LGBTQ Historic Sites Project and Making Gay History have built a digital 3D model of the bar as it stood that year — two separate rooms divided by a wall, controlled entry points, a small tucked-away bar in back, all details lost to decades of renovation. It's the most in-depth reconstruction of the Stonewall interior ever created, a way to stand inside a piece of history that no longer physically exists.

stories.title: How a ‘living breakwater’ in Hawai‘i aims to create coral habitat and protect coastline
stories.summary: Off the coast of Oʻahu, researchers are sinking 60 massive concrete structures into the ocean to build a 'living breakwater' — an artificial hybrid reef designed to absorb storm waves and create new coral habitat at the same time.
stories.extended_summary: Each structure weighs 4 metric tons, and 60 of them are being lowered 210 feet off Kalaeloa Harbor into the waters off West Oʻahu. It's the first artificial hybrid reef designed specifically to protect coastlines — absorbing the wave energy that increasingly intense storms slam into Hawaiʻi's shores, while simultaneously creating new habitat for coral. As of late October, eight were in place, floated out on a special shallow-water catamaran. The project is backed by $27 million from DARPA, the Defense Department's research arm, and it's testing an unusual idea: that the best seawall might be a living one.

stories.title: How did this town become 'Halloween Capital of the World?'
stories.summary: In 1919, Anoka, Minnesota's teens ran so wild — tipping an occupied outhouse, releasing cattle, hoisting wagons onto roofs — that the town threw a supervised Halloween party to contain them. It worked so well that Anoka has called itself the 'Halloween Capital of the World' ever since.
stories.extended_summary: The tipping point, allegedly, was the outhouse — flipped with someone still inside. In 1919, the youths of Anoka, Minnesota, were terrorizing the town with pranks: cattle set loose, wagons stranded on rooftops, general mayhem. So the town tried something different — a 'supervised Halloween frolic' with costume contests, live-chicken scrambles, a night parade, and a street dance. It worked. More than 1,000 costumed kids turned out, and the Minneapolis Journal reported that 'ash cans and back gates were undisturbed for the first time in the community's history.' Within a few years Anoka had crowned itself the Halloween Capital of the World — a title it has defended, with considerable civic pride, for over a century.

stories.title: How one local nonprofit is working to protect creative spaces for artists in Greater Boston
stories.summary: Greater Boston has lost more than 2 million square feet of artist space in a decade. Now the Arts & Business Council of Greater Boston is building a creative land trust to buy and protect studios before artists get priced out — a nonprofit workaround while cities wait on legislation.
stories.extended_summary: More than 2 million square feet of artist studios, rehearsal rooms and production space have vanished from Greater Boston in the last decade. Somerville wants to fight back with a land trust that buys properties to keep artists in place — but municipalities can't legally establish one by right, and the fix could take years. So nonprofits are stepping in. Jim Grace, executive director of the Arts & Business Council of Greater Boston, runs its creative land trust, buying space in a state with steep rents and a housing shortage. "The forces of gentrification, increased prices are never really gonna slow down," he said. "If there's no space to make art, it is going to impact the entire ecosystem of the arts."

stories.title: Hunting for a Cooking Oil Replacement in Pennsylvania’s Forests
stories.summary: Pennsylvania's bitternut hickory trees are hiding a pantry staple: cooking oil. A growing network of gatherers and processors is pressing local nut oil to replace imported olive, canola and palm — and the U.S. spent $10.9 billion on vegetable oil imports in 2022 alone. One nut-gathering event at a time.
stories.extended_summary: The U.S. spent $10.9 billion importing cooking oil in 2022 — while bitternut hickory trees dropped an untapped oil crop across Pennsylvania and the East Coast. "We have this staple oil crop on the East Coast of North America that no one looks at as oil," said Brian Nana-Sinkam of Third Place Processing in Oley, Pennsylvania, where presses extract edible oil from hickory nuts. A small but growing network of gatherers, farmers, processors and tree breeders is determined to make hickory oil a pantry staple, pushing back against a global industry built on mass shipping and deforestation. The obstacles are real: low public awareness and limited resources. So they're starting with one nut-gathering event at a time.
